title: PostgreSQL max_connections exhausted
symptoms: Prometheus alert: postgresql_max_connections_exhausted
Grafana dashboard: PostgreSQL Metrics -> 'Max Connections Used' metric spikes to 100%
User-facing issues: delayed or failed transactions, increased latency in payment processing
diagnosis_steps: step 1: `kubectl exec -it <postgres-pod> -- psql -c 'SHOW max_connections;'` to check current max_connections setting
step 2: `kubectl exec -it <postgres-pod> -- psql -c 'SELECT usename, count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY usename ORDER BY count DESC;'` to identify high-usage connections
step 3: Decision point - if max_connections is reached and high-usage connections are identified, proceed to resolution steps
resolution_steps: step 1: `kubectl exec -it <postgres-pod> -- psql -c 'SET max_connections = 200;'` to increase max_connections temporarily
step 2: Monitor for stability and performance; if issues persist, consider scaling PostgreSQL resources
step 3: `kubectl exec -it <postgres-pod> -- psql -c 'SHOW max_connections;'` to verify new setting
escalation: When to escalate: If max_connections is consistently reached and increasing it does not resolve the issue, page the SRE on-call. Specific threshold: 95% max_connections usage for 10 consecutive minutes.
rollback: Exact rollback procedure: `kubectl exec -it <postgres-pod> -- psql -c 'SET max_connections = 150;'` to revert to previous setting if the increase makes the situation worse.
prevention: Specific technical improvement to prevent recurrence: Implement connection pooling in application services to reduce the number of concurrent database connections and monitor application performance to optimize resource usage.
related_alerts: Grafana dashboard: PostgreSQL Metrics -> 'Max Connections Used'

title: PostgreSQL disk full on WAL directory
symptoms: Prometheus alert: 'postgres_wal_directory_usage' exceeds 80%
Grafana dashboard: 'PostgreSQL WAL Directory Usage' shows >80% usage
User facing issues: Payment processing delays or failures
diagnosis_steps: kubectl exec -it <postgres-pod> -- psql -c "SELECT * FROM pg_stat_wal_;"
Check the output for 'location' and 'written' to identify the current WAL usage
If usage is high, decide on the next steps: increase storage, optimize WAL archiving, or scale out
resolution_steps: kubectl exec -it <postgres-pod> -- psql -c "SELECT pg_stop_backup();"
Scale out the PostgreSQL deployment to add more storage
Verify with 'kubectl exec -it <postgres-pod> -- psql -c "SELECT * FROM pg_stat_wal_;"' that usage has decreased
escalation: If the issue persists and usage continues to rise, escalate to the SRE lead at FinTechFlow when 'postgres_wal_directory_usage' exceeds 90%
rollback: If the fix makes the situation worse, rollback to the previous state by restoring from a backup and scaling back the deployment
prevention: Implement automated WAL archiving and regular storage capacity checks to prevent future issues

title: PostgreSQL replication lag exceeded threshold
symptoms: Prometheus alert: `postgresql_replication_lag_seconds{instance="replica-instance"} > 60`
Grafana dashboard: `Replication Lag` panel shows > 60 seconds lag
User facing impact: Transaction processing delays or failures
diagnosis_steps: step 1: `kubectl exec -it postgresql-replica-0 -- psql -c "SHOW replica_identity"` to check replica identity
step 2: Look for output indicating `replica_identity` is set correctly, if not, it may be a configuration issue
step 3: If replica identity is correct, check `kubectl get pods -l app=postgresql -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.containerStatuses[0].ready}'` to ensure the replica pod is healthy
resolution_steps: step 1: `kubectl exec -it postgresql-replica-0 -- psql -c "SELECT * FROM pg_stat_replication"` to check replication status
step 2: If replication is lagging, restart the replica pod with `kubectl delete pod postgresql-replica-0`
step 3: `kubectl get pods -l app=postgresql -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.phase}'` to verify the new replica is running and healthy
escalation: escalate to on-call SRE team if the lag persists after 15 minutes, page `payments-sre` team
rollback: exact rollback procedure: `kubectl replace -f <replica-pod-definition.yaml>` with the previous working definition, then restart the pod
prevention: implement automatic failover and health checks for PostgreSQL replicas, and regularly review and update PostgreSQL configuration

title: PostgreSQL backup job failing silently
symptoms: specific symptom 1 as seen in Prometheus or PagerDuty: backup job duration spikes to 0 seconds and no new backup files appear in the backup directory.
specific symptom 2 with metric name or log pattern: 'pg_basebackup failed with error: <error_message>' in the Kubernetes pod logs.
specific symptom 3 user facing impact: No impact to users, but the backup job is not functioning as expected, which could lead to data loss in case of a disaster.
diagnosis_steps: step 1: `kubectl -n <namespace> logs <pod-name>` to check the PostgreSQL backup pod logs for any error messages.
step 2: `kubectl -n <namespace> exec <pod-name> -- psql -c "SELECT * FROM pg_stat_wal_receiver;"` to check the status of the WAL receiver.

step 3: Decision point - If the logs indicate a connection issue or an error with pg_basebackup, proceed with resolution steps. If the issue is with the PostgreSQL instance, contact the database team.
resolution_steps: step 1: `kubectl -n <namespace> exec <pod-name> -- pg_basebackup -h <hostname> -D /var/lib/postgresql/backup -U <username> -P <password> -Fp` to manually run the backup command.
step 2: Verify the backup files in the backup directory and ensure they are not corrupted.
step 3: `kubectl -n <namespace> exec <pod-name> -- psql -c "SELECT * FROM pg_wal_summary;"` to check the status of the WAL receiver and ensure it is running correctly.
escalation: When to escalate: If the issue persists after manual intervention, escalate to the database team. Page the on-call SREs at FinTechFlow.
rollback: Exact rollback procedure if fix makes situation worse: Stop the faulty backup job, revert to the last known good backup, and restart the backup job.
prevention: Specific technical improvement to prevent recurrence: Implement a monitoring solution to alert on backup job failures and ensure regular health checks of the PostgreSQL instance and backup process.
related_alerts: PromQL alert name or Grafana dashboard name 1: `pg_backup_job_duration{job="pg_backup"} > 5`

title: PostgreSQL slow queries causing timeout cascade
symptoms: High CPU usage on PostgreSQL pods as seen in Prometheus
Error logs in Kubernetes cluster showing slow query timeouts
User reports delayed or failed transactions through merchant API
diagnosis_steps: step 1: kubectl -n <namespace> get pods -l app=postgres -o wide; psql -h <pod_ip> -U <username> -d <database> -c "SELECT * FROM pg_stat_statements WHERE calls > 10 AND total_time > 1000 ORDER BY total_time DESC;"
step 2: Look for queries with high total_time and calls; check the query execution plans and indexes
step 3: If slow queries are identified, decide whether to optimize queries or scale resources
resolution_steps: step 1: Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE <slow_query> to understand the execution plan and identify bottlenecks
step 2: Optimize the slow query or add indexes, then verify with EXPLAIN ANALYZE
step 3: Scale PostgreSQL resources if necessary, using kubectl scale deployment <postgres-deployment> --replicas=<new_replicas>
escalation: If the query optimization or scaling does not resolve the issue within 30 minutes, page the SRE team lead or on-call SRE.
rollback: If the fix makes the situation worse, rollback to the previous state by reverting the changes in Kubernetes and monitoring for a short period.
prevention: Implement query monitoring and optimization policies, and regularly review and optimize database queries.

title: PostgreSQL streaming replication slot bloat
symptoms: High CPU usage on the PostgreSQL replica as seen in Prometheus
Increased latency in read operations from the replica with metric name `db.replica.latency`
Users experiencing delays or errors in read operations from the replica
diagnosis_steps: step 1: Run `SELECT * FROM pg_stat_replication;` to check for active replication slots
step 2: Look for slots with high `active` status and large `active_xmin` values
step 3: If a slot is found with high `active_xmin` and `active` status, it indicates bloat
resolution_steps: step 1: Run `SELECT pg_drop_replication_slot('slot_name');` to drop the problematic slot
step 2: Monitor the `pg_stat_replication` view to ensure the slot has been dropped
step 3: Verify the replica's health with `pg_is.replica` and `pg_wal_size`
escalation: If the bloat persists or causes significant performance degradation, escalate to the SRE on-call at FinTechFlow
rollback: If the resolution makes the situation worse, revert the `pg_drop_replication_slot` command and monitor the replica health closely
prevention: Implement automated scripts to regularly check and drop inactive replication slots

title: PostgreSQL sequence overflow risk
symptoms: High CPU usage on PostgreSQL nodes as seen in Prometheus
Error messages in PostgreSQL logs such as 'sequence overflow'
Decreased performance and potential service downtime affecting users
diagnosis_steps: step 1: Run `kubectl get pods -n <namespace>` to identify affected PostgreSQL pods
step 2: Use `kubectl exec -it <pod_name> -n <namespace> -- psql -c 'SELECT * FROM information_schema.sequences WHERE sequence_name LIKE 'your_sequence_name''` to check sequence status
step 3: If sequence overflow is confirmed, check the application logs for related transactions
resolution_steps: step 1: Increase the sequence's maximum value with `ALTER SEQUENCE <sequence_name> RESTART WITH <new_max_value>;`
step 2: Monitor the application for any issues post-restart
step 3: Verify with `SELECT nextval('<sequence_name>')` that the sequence has been correctly reset
escalation: If the issue persists or affects more than 10% of transactions, page the on-call engineer at FinTechFlow
rollback: If the fix makes the situation worse, revert the sequence change using `ALTER SEQUENCE <sequence_name> RESTART WITH <original_max_value>;` and monitor for any additional issues
prevention: Implement sequence health checks as part of regular database maintenance and set up alerts in Prometheus and Grafana

title: Redis maxmemory eviction storm

increased eviction rate in Redis logs
slow performance and timeouts in application services

step 3: Decision point - if eviction rate is high and memory usage is close to max, proceed to resolution

step 2: Follow up with capacity planning and scaling of Redis deployment
step 3: `kubectl exec -it <redis-pod> -n <namespace> -- redis-cli info memory` to verify new settings and healthy output
escalation: If the issue persists and causes service degradation, escalate to P2 severity and page on-call SREs and senior leadership
rollback: If the fix makes the situation worse, revert to previous configuration using `kubectl edit configmap <redis-configmap> -n <namespace>` and monitor for further issues
prevention: Implement automated monitoring for Redis memory usage and evictions, and set up alerts in Prometheus and Grafana
related_alerts: Grafana dashboard: Redis Memory Usage and Evictions

title: Redis cluster node failure and failover
symptoms: specific symptom 1 as seen in Prometheus or PagerDuty: 'redis_cluster_node_down' alert firing
specific symptom 2 with metric name or log pattern: 'redis_cluster_node_failure' log pattern in EKS cluster logs
specific symptom 3 user facing impact: Increased latency in payment-service and order-service
diagnosis_steps: step 1: exact kubectl, psql, redis-cli or AWS CLI command to run: `kubectl get pods -n <namespace>` to check running pods
step 2: what output to look for and what it means: Look for any pods in a 'CrashLoopBackOff' state or with 'Terminating' status
step 3: decision point - what determines next action: If a node is down, proceed to the resolution steps
resolution_steps: step 1: exact remediation command with explanation: `kubectl delete pod <pod-name> -n <namespace>` to restart the pod
step 2: follow-up action: Check the pod's logs using `kubectl logs <pod-name> -n <namespace>` for any error messages

step 3: verification command and expected healthy output: `kubectl get pods -n <namespace>` should show all pods in 'Running' state and `redis-cli -h <master-ip> -p 6379 cluster nodes` should show all nodes in the cluster
escalation: when to escalate: If the node failure persists and affects more than 50% of the cluster, page the on-call SRE team
rollback: exact rollback procedure if fix makes situation worse: `kubectl rollout undo deployment/<service-deployment-name> -n <namespace>` to revert to the previous deployment version
prevention: specific technical improvement to prevent recurrence: Implement automatic node replacement in the Kubernetes cluster using StatefulSets and DaemonSets
related_alerts: PromQL alert name or Grafana dashboard name 1: 'redis_cluster_node_down'

title: Redis sentinel failover not completing
symptoms: Specific symptom 1 as seen in Prometheus or PagerDuty: High latency or increased error rate in Redis operations.
Specific symptom 2 with metric name or log pattern: Redis Sentinel failover state showing 'failover-not-complete' in Prometheus metrics or log messages indicating failure to promote a new master.
Specific symptom 3 user facing impact: Payment processing delays or failures due to Redis unavailability.
diagnosis_steps: Step 1: Run `kubectl get pods -l app=redis-sentinel` to check the status of Redis sentinel pods.
Step 2: Check the output for any pods in a 'CrashLoopBackOff' state or with 'Last State' showing 'terminated' with exit code 137 (memory issue) or 1 (general error).
Step 3: Decision point - If a sentinel pod is in a 'CrashLoopBackOff' state, proceed to step 4; otherwise, check the logs using `kubectl logs <pod-name> -c <container-name>` for errors.
resolution_steps: Step 1: Execute `kubectl delete pod <pod-name> -c <container-name>` to forcefully delete the failing sentinel pod and allow Kubernetes to recreate it.
Step 2: Follow-up action: Monitor the system for any further issues and ensure the new sentinel pod is functioning correctly.
Step 3: Run `redis-cli sentinel master <master-name>` to check the current state of the master and verify that the failover is complete.
escalation: When to escalate: If the failover does not complete within 30 minutes, page the on-call SRE team and senior management.
rollback: Exact rollback procedure if fix makes situation worse: If the new sentinel pod fails to resolve the issue, revert to the previous working state by rolling back the deployment and monitoring for any regressions.
prevention: Specific technical improvement to prevent recurrence: Implement automatic scaling for Redis sentinel pods based on resource usage and configure proper resource limits to prevent memory issues.
related_alerts: PromQL alert name or Grafana dashboard name 1: 'redis_sentinel_failover_timeout'

title: Redis cache stampede after flush
symptoms: specific symptom 1 as seen in Prometheus or PagerDuty: Increased request latency and error rate in payment-service and order-service
specific symptom 2 with metric name or log pattern: High CPU and I/O usage reported by Prometheus for Redis pods
specific symptom 3 user facing impact: Delayed payment processing and order confirmation for merchants
diagnosis_steps: step 1: exact kubectl, psql, redis-cli or AWS CLI command to run: `kubectl get pods -n redis; kubectl exec -it <redis-pod-name> -n redis -- redis-cli info`
step 2: what output to look for and what it means: Check `used_memory` and `used_memory_peak` to see if they are abnormally high, and `connected_clients` to see if there are many clients connected
step 3: decision point - what determines next action: If `used_memory` is significantly higher than usual and `connected_clients` are high, proceed to resolution steps
resolution_steps: step 1: exact remediation command with explanation: `kubectl exec -it <redis-pod-name> -n redis -- redis-cli flushall` to flush the cache, and `kubectl scale deployment <redis-deployment-name> -n redis --replicas=0` and `--replicas=1` to restart the Redis pod
step 2: follow-up action: Monitor the Redis pod for any errors or issues after restart

step 3: verification command and expected healthy output: `kubectl exec -it <redis-pod-name> -n redis -- redis-cli info` should show normal memory usage and connected clients, and `kubectl get pods -n redis` should show the Redis pod is running without errors
escalation: when to escalate: specific threshold and who to page at FinTechFlow: If the issue persists or worsens, page the on-call SRE or the team lead
rollback: exact rollback procedure if fix makes situation worse: `kubectl scale deployment <redis-deployment-name> -n redis --replicas=0` and `--replicas=<previous-replica-count>` to revert the changes
prevention: specific technical improvement to prevent recurrence: Implement rate limiting and retry mechanisms in the services using Redis to prevent stampedes, and consider using a more robust caching strategy
related_alerts: PromQL alert name or Grafana dashboard name 1: `redis_memory_usage_high`

title: Redis AOF rewrite causing disk I/O saturation
symptoms: High disk I/O usage as seen in Prometheus metrics
Errors in Redis logs indicating AOF rewrite process
User facing issues such as delayed notifications or payment processing
diagnosis_steps: Step 1: Run `kubectl get pods -n <namespace>` to identify the Redis pod experiencing issues
Step 2: Execute `kubectl exec -it <redis-pod-name> -n <namespace> -- redis-cli info` and look for `aof_rewrite_in_progress` and `used_memory_rss`
Step 3: If `aof_rewrite_in_progress` is true and `used_memory_rss` is high, decide to scale Redis or adjust AOF settings
resolution_steps: Step 1: Scale Redis deployment by running `kubectl scale deployment <redis-deployment-name> --replicas=<new-replica-count> -n <namespace>`
Step 2: Monitor the situation and consider adjusting Redis AOF settings such as `appendfsync everysec`
Step 3: Verify the resolution by checking `kubectl exec -it <redis-pod-name> -n <namespace> -- redis-cli info` for reduced `used_memory_rss` and no `aof_rewrite_in_progress`
escalation: If the issue persists and causes disk I/O to exceed 80% for more than 15 minutes, page the on-call SRE team and key stakeholders.
rollback: If the fix makes the situation worse, rollback to the previous state by scaling down the Redis deployment and reverting AOF settings to their original values.
prevention: Implement monitoring for AOF rewrite frequency and size, and set up automated scaling policies based on disk I/O usage.

title: Elasticsearch heap exhaustion
symptoms: Heap usage alerts in Prometheus with metric name `elasticsearch_heap_used_in_bytes` exceeding 90%
Elasticsearch log patterns indicating `heap space exhaustion` or `GC overhead limit exceeded`
User facing impact including slower search queries and potential service downtime
diagnosis_steps: step 1: `kubectl get pods -n es` to identify the affected Elasticsearch pod
step 2: `kubectl exec -it <pod-name> -n es -- curl -XGET 'http://localhost:9200/_nodes/stats/jvm?pretty'` to check JVM heap statistics
step 3: Decision point - if JVM heap usage is above 90% or GC overhead is high, proceed to resolution
resolution_steps: step 1: `kubectl exec -it <pod-name> -n es -- curl -XPUT 'http://localhost:9200/_cluster/settings' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"transient": {"cluster.routing.allocation.enable": "none"}}'` to pause allocation for 10 minutes
step 2: Increase JVM heap size using `kubectl edit statefulset <statefulset-name> -n es` and add or modify `resources.limits` and `resources.requests` for `heap`

step 3: `kubectl exec -it <pod-name> -n es -- curl -XPUT 'http://localhost:9200/_cluster/settings' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"transient": {"cluster.routing.allocation.enable": "all"}}'` to resume allocation
escalation: When JVM heap usage exceeds 95% or GC overhead limit is triggered, page the on-call SRE
rollback: If the fix makes the situation worse, revert the change by halting the statefulset edit and reverting the `heap` settings
prevention: Implement automatic monitoring and alerts for Elasticsearch heap usage, and regularly review and adjust resource limits

title: Elasticsearch index corruption recovery
symptoms: specific symptom 1 as seen in Prometheus or PagerDuty: Elasticsearch cluster health status shows yellow or red.
specific symptom 2 with metric name or log pattern: Elasticsearch logs show errors like 'index corruption detected' or 'data recovery failed'.
specific symptom 3 user facing impact: Users report delays or failures in transaction processing.
diagnosis_steps: step 1: kubectl get pods -n es-cluster -l app=elasticsearch to check the status of Elasticsearch pods.
step 2: kubectl logs <pod-name> -n es-cluster to view logs for specific pod and look for error messages related to index corruption.
step 3: kubectl exec -it <pod-name> -n es-cluster -- /usr/share/elasticsearch/bin/elasticsearch-keystore list to check if any critical settings are missing or altered.
resolution_steps: step 1: kubectl exec -it <pod-name> -n es-cluster -- /usr/share/elasticsearch/bin/elasticsearch-reset-password --anonymize to reset any compromised passwords.
step 2: Follow the steps in the Elasticsearch documentation to perform a recovery from a backup or reindexing if necessary.
step 3: kubectl exec -it <pod-name> -n es-cluster -- /usr/share/elasticsearch/bin/elasticsearch-keystore list to verify that all critical settings are correctly set.
escalation: when to escalate: If the issue persists after the initial steps and affects more than 10% of the transactions, page the on-call SRE. Specific threshold: 10% transaction failure rate. Who to page: On-call SRE at FinTechFlow.
rollback: exact rollback procedure if fix makes situation worse: If the reindexing or recovery process causes further issues, revert to the last known good state using a backup from before the corruption was detected.
prevention: specific technical improvement to prevent recurrence: Implement regular automated backups and use snapshot and restore procedures. Ensure that critical settings are stored in a secure location and are not manually altered.
related_alerts: PromQL alert name or Grafana dashboard name 1: es_cluster_health_status_alert

title: Elasticsearch cluster split-brain recovery
symptoms: specific symptom 1 as seen in Prometheus or PagerDuty: Elasticsearch cluster health shows yellow or red status
specific symptom 2 with metric name or log pattern: Elasticsearch cluster logs show 'split brain' or 'master not found' errors
specific symptom 3 user facing impact: Increased latency or failure in transaction processing and order fulfillment
diagnosis_steps: step 1: kubectl get pods -n <namespace> -o wide to check Elasticsearch pod status and IP addresses
step 2: kubectl logs <pod_name> -n <namespace> to check Elasticsearch logs for 'split brain' or 'master not found' errors
step 3: decision point - if the master node is lost or if there are conflicting master nodes, proceed to resolution steps

step 2: follow-up action: wait for the Elasticsearch cluster to recover and check cluster health using kubectl exec -it <master_pod> -n <namespace> -- /usr/share/elasticsearch/bin/elasticsearch-cluster-health
step 3: verification command and expected healthy output: kubectl exec -it <master_pod> -n <namespace> -- /usr/share/elasticsearch/bin/elasticsearch-cluster-health --wait-for-green-status
escalation: when to escalate: if the cluster does not recover within 30 minutes, page the on-call SRE and SRE lead
rollback: exact rollback procedure if fix makes situation worse: revert the reset-primary-shards command and follow the recovery steps for a failed master node
prevention: specific technical improvement to prevent recurrence: implement Elasticsearch cluster health monitoring and alerts, and ensure proper quorum settings
related_alerts: PromQL alert name or Grafana dashboard name 1: elasticsearch_cluster_health

symptoms: specific symptom 1 as seen in Prometheus or PagerDuty: 'kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total' metric shows high restarts for the affected pod
specific symptom 2 with metric name or log pattern: 'CrashLoopBackOff' events logged in the Kubernetes event stream
specific symptom 3 user facing impact: Users may experience delays or failures in payment processing
diagnosis_steps: step 1: exact kubectl, psql, redis-cli or AWS CLI command to run: `kubectl describe pod <pod-name>` and `kubectl logs <pod-name> -c <container-name>`

step 2: what output to look for and what it means: Look for error messages, stack traces, or other clues in the logs that indicate the cause of the crash. Check the container logs for any error messages or exceptions.

step 3: decision point - what determines next action: If the issue is related to a configuration problem, update the deployment. If it's a code issue, redeploy the container image. If it's a resource constraint, scale the deployment or adjust resource limits.
resolution_steps: step 1: exact remediation command with explanation: `kubectl set image deployment/<deployment-name> <container-name>=<new-image-version>` to update the container image, or `kubectl scale deployment/<deployment-name> --replicas=<new-replica-count>` to adjust the number of replicas
step 2: follow-up action: Verify that the issue has been resolved by monitoring the pod's status and logs. Ensure that the pod is no longer in CrashLoopBackOff state.

step 3: verification command and expected healthy output: `kubectl get pods -o wide` should show the pod in a Running state, and `kubectl logs <pod-name> -c <container-name>` should not show any error messages.
escalation: when to escalate: If the issue persists after the first resolution attempt, escalate to the platform-sre lead or senior SRE. Specific threshold: If the issue affects more than 10% of the pods in a service and lasts for more than 1 hour, page the on-call team.
rollback: exact rollback procedure if fix makes situation worse: `kubectl rollout undo deployment/<deployment-name>` to revert the deployment to the previous version. Monitor the affected pods to ensure the rollback is successful.
prevention: specific technical improvement to prevent recurrence: Implement a comprehensive logging and monitoring strategy to capture and analyze logs in real-time. Use automated deployment pipelines with pre-deployment checks to ensure that only healthy images are deployed. Implement resource requests and limits to prevent resource starvation.
related_alerts: PromQL alert name or Grafana dashboard name 1: 'KubernetesPodCrashLoopBackOffAlert'

title: ArgoCD sync failure recovery
symptoms: specific symptom 1 as seen in Prometheus or PagerDuty: ArgoCD sync job status shows as 'failed' or 'error' in the ArgoCD UI or Prometheus alerts.
specific symptom 2 with metric name or log pattern: `argocd_sync_status` metric shows 'failed' or `kubectl logs argocd-sync` shows errors related to syncing repositories.
specific symptom 3 user facing impact: Users may experience service outages or degraded performance if the failed sync impacts critical services.
diagnosis_steps: step 1: `kubectl get pods -n argocd` to check if ArgoCD components are running.
step 2: `kubectl logs argocd-sync -n argocd` to identify the specific error message.
step 3: Decision point - if the error is due to network issues, escalate to network team; if it's a configuration issue, escalate to DevOps team.
resolution_steps: step 1: `kubectl delete pods -n argocd argocd-sync` to restart the sync job.
step 2: Monitor the sync job for successful completion.
step 3: `kubectl get pods -n argocd` to ensure all ArgoCD components are running and `argocd sync status` to confirm the repository sync is successful.
escalation: When to escalate: If the sync failure persists after restarting, escalate to the platform-sre team lead. Specific threshold: If the sync failure impacts more than 3 services. Who to page: platform-sre team lead and on-call SRE.
rollback: Exact rollback procedure if fix makes situation worse: `kubectl rollout undo deployment/<affected-deployment> -n <namespace>` to revert to the previous deployment version.
prevention: Specific technical improvement to prevent recurrence: Implement a monitoring alert for ArgoCD sync failures and ensure regular backups of ArgoCD repositories.
related_alerts: PromQL alert name or Grafana dashboard name 1: argocd_sync_status_alert

title: etcd high latency risk mitigation
symptoms: etcd leader election latency spikes > 10 seconds as seen in Prometheus
etcd request latency > 500ms for critical operations in Grafana dashboard
User facing payment processing delays or failures
diagnosis_steps: step 1: Run `kubectl get etcdcluster -n <namespace>` to check etcd cluster health
step 2: Check etcd leader election latency with `curl http://<etcd-leader-ip>:2379/v2/keys/etcd-cluster/leader`
step 3: Evaluate if the high latency is due to network issues by running `kubectl exec -it <etcd-pod> -- /bin/bash -c 'etcdctl endpoint health'`
resolution_steps: step 1: Scale up etcd nodes by running `kubectl scale statefulset etcd -n <namespace> --replicas=<new-replicas>`
step 2: Monitor the etcd cluster for stability and adjust the number of replicas if necessary
step 3: Verify the resolution with `kubectl get etcdcluster -n <namespace>` and check for healthy etcd nodes
escalation: If the etcd leader election latency remains > 10 seconds for more than 10 minutes, page the on-call SRE team and escalate to senior management
rollback: Roll back to previous etcd configuration by scaling down the etcd nodes and reverting the changes if the issue persists after the initial resolution
prevention: Implement etcd cluster health monitoring and auto-scaling policies, and regularly review etcd configuration for optimal performance

title: PodDisruptionBudget emergency override
symptoms: High alert count in Prometheus for `kubernetes_pod_disruption_budget_status_unhealthy`
Metric `kubernetes_pod_disruption_budget_status_unhealthy` shows a significant increase
User facing issues such as delayed or failed transactions
diagnosis_steps: step 1: `kubectl get poddisruptionbudgets -n <namespace>` to identify affected PDB
step 2: Check the output for the `status` and `allowedDisruptions` fields
step 3: Decision point - if the allowed disruptions are exhausted, proceed with override
resolution_steps: step 1: `kubectl patch poddisruptionbudget <pdb-name> -n <namespace> --patch '{"spec":{"maxUnavailable":0}}'` to override the PDB
step 2: Monitor the `allowedDisruptions` and `currentDisruptions` fields to ensure the override is effective
step 3: `kubectl get pods -n <namespace>` to verify that the pods are now being scheduled
escalation: When the `allowedDisruptions` count reaches 0 and the override is required, page the on-call SREs and the SRE lead
rollback: If the override causes issues, revert by running `kubectl patch poddisruptionbudget <pdb-name> -n <namespace> --patch '{"spec":{"maxUnavailable":"<original-value>"}}'`
prevention: Review and adjust the PDB configurations to ensure they align with the desired disruption budget

title: EKS control plane API server degradation
symptoms: High CPU utilization or response time for API server requests as seen in Prometheus or Grafana
Prolonged API server unavailability or errors in Kubernetes cluster status as logged in AWS CloudWatch
User facing payment processing delays or failures
diagnosis_steps: step 1: `kubectl get nodes` to check node status, look for any nodes in unschedulable state
step 2: `kubectl get cs` to inspect control plane component status, check for any errors or degraded states
step 3: Evaluate if the issue is related to resource constraints or network issues
resolution_steps: step 1: `aws eks update-kubeconfig --region <region> --name <cluster-name>` to ensure the latest cluster configuration is used
step 2: Scale up the control plane nodes if necessary, e.g., `eksctl scale nodegroup --cluster <cluster-name> --nodes-min 3 --nodes-max 5 --node-type t3.large`
step 3: Validate the resolution with `kubectl get cs` and monitor for any further issues
escalation: If the issue persists or affects more than 10% of the transaction volume, escalate to the on-call SRE team and PagerDuty
rollback: If the fix exacerbates the situation, revert the changes using `eksctl delete nodegroup --cluster <cluster-name> --name <nodegroup-name>` and scale back to previous node configuration
prevention: Implement automated monitoring and alerting for control plane resource utilization, and regularly review and update the node group configurations

step 3: `kubectl get pods -n <namespace>` to verify the new number of replicas and their status
